insulin-first-treatment.title: Insulin is first used to treat diabetes
insulin-first-treatment.text: In Toronto, Frederick Banting and Charles Best, with James Collip and John Macleod, made an extract of the pancreas containing insulin, a peptide hormone. Clinical tests by January 1922 showed that it lowered blood sugar in people with diabetes, and the team published its first clinical report in March 1922.

nobel-1923-insulin.title: Nobel Prize for the discovery of insulin
nobel-1923-insulin.text: Frederick Banting and John Macleod received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1923 'for the discovery of insulin'.

us-food-drug-cosmetic-act-1938.title: US law starts to require proof of safety
us-food-drug-cosmetic-act-1938.text: In 1937 a medicine called Elixir of Sulfanilamide, dissolved in the toxic solvent diethylene glycol, killed 107 people, many of them children. The US Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, approved on 25 June 1938, then required new drugs to be shown safe before marketing. It did not yet require proof that they work.

oxytocin-synthesis.title: The first peptide hormone made in a laboratory
oxytocin-synthesis.text: Vincent du Vigneaud's group made oxytocin from its building blocks and showed that the synthetic version acted like the natural hormone. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1955 for 'the first synthesis of a polypeptide hormone'.

insulin-structure.title: Sanger works out the structure of insulin
insulin-structure.text: Frederick Sanger's group worked out the order of the amino acids in insulin's two chains, and in 1955 reported how the chains are joined by disulphide bonds. Sanger received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1958 for this work.

nl-wog-1958.title: Dutch medicines law sets up a register
nl-wog-1958.text: The Wet op de Geneesmiddelenvoorziening of 28 July 1958 set up a board to register packaged medicines in the Netherlands. A product could be registered if it could reasonably be assumed to have the claimed effect and not to harm health when used as directed. Selling unregistered packaged medicines was forbidden.

thalidomide-withdrawn.title: Thalidomide is withdrawn after severe birth defects
thalidomide-withdrawn.text: Thalidomide, a sedative sold in 46 countries and given for morning sickness, caused severe birth defects in more than 10,000 children between 1957 and 1962. Doctors in Germany and Australia linked it to the defects in 1961, and withdrawals began in November 1961. In the US, the FDA reviewer Frances Kelsey had refused to approve it because the evidence was inadequate.

kefauver-harris-1962.title: US law starts to require proof that a medicine works
kefauver-harris-1962.text: On 10 October 1962 the Kefauver-Harris Drug Amendments became US law. Companies now had to provide substantial evidence of effectiveness from adequate and well-controlled studies before approval. Trial participants had to be told and asked for consent, with some exceptions.

solid-phase-synthesis.title: A faster way to build peptides
solid-phase-synthesis.text: Bruce Merrifield described solid-phase peptide synthesis: the first amino acid is anchored to a solid support, the chain is built one amino acid at a time, and by-products are washed away after each step. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1984.

eu-directive-65-65.title: Europe's first medicines law
eu-directive-65-65.text: Council Directive 65/65/EEC of 26 January 1965 said that no ready-made medicine may be placed on the market in a member state of the European Economic Community without an authorisation. Applicants had to submit test results, including clinical trials, and a licence was refused if the medicine was harmful or its effect was lacking or not properly shown. The European Commission says the thalidomide disaster was much of the impetus.

gnrh-sequence.title: The structure of a brain peptide that controls fertility
gnrh-sequence.text: Andrew Schally's group proposed the amino-acid sequence of a hormone from the pig hypothalamus that releases LH and FSH from the pituitary gland, known today as GnRH. Leuprolide, approved in 1985, is a lab-made analogue of this hormone.

somatostatin-discovery.title: Somatostatin is discovered
somatostatin-discovery.text: Roger Guillemin's group isolated a 14-amino-acid peptide from sheep hypothalamus that blocked the release of growth hormone in lab tests and in rats, and showed that a synthetic copy works too. It became known as somatostatin.

nobel-1977-peptide-hormones.title: Nobel Prize for peptide hormones of the brain
nobel-1977-peptide-hormones.text: Roger Guillemin and Andrew Schally shared half of the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1977 for discoveries about the peptide hormones made by the brain. Rosalyn Yalow received the other half for radioimmunoassays, tests that could measure peptide hormones in blood.

recombinant-human-insulin.title: First medicine made with recombinant DNA
recombinant-human-insulin.text: On 28 October 1982, after five months of review, the FDA approved Humulin, human insulin made by bacteria that had been given the genetic code for its two chains. It was the first approved medical product of any kind made with this technology.

leuprolide-approval.title: A GnRH analogue is approved
leuprolide-approval.text: On 9 April 1985 the FDA approved Lupron (leuprolide), a lab-made analogue of GnRH. Given continuously, it first raises the sex hormones and then lowers them.

glp1-insulin-release.title: GLP-1 is shown to release insulin
glp1-insulin-release.text: Three groups showed that a fragment of proglucagon made in the gut, GLP-1, releases insulin: in pig pancreas, in rat pancreas, and in seven human volunteers. This hormone is the basis of medicines such as semaglutide and tirzepatide.

octreotide-approval.title: A long-acting somatostatin analogue is approved
octreotide-approval.text: On 21 October 1988 the FDA approved Sandostatin (octreotide), an eight-amino-acid analogue of somatostatin. In lab tests it resisted breakdown, and in rats and monkeys it acted much longer than the natural hormone.

exendin-4-discovery.title: A peptide is found in lizard venom
exendin-4-discovery.text: John Eng's group isolated exendin-4 from the venom of the Gila monster. A synthetic version, exenatide, later became a medicine that acts on the GLP-1 receptor.

us-accelerated-approval.title: US accelerated approval and user fees
us-accelerated-approval.text: In 1992 the FDA formalised accelerated approval: a medicine for a serious disease can be approved on an early sign of benefit, such as tumour shrinkage, if the company later confirms a real clinical benefit. The same year a new law required companies to pay user fees, so the FDA could hire more reviewers and speed up reviews.

ema-founded.title: A European medicines agency is founded
ema-founded.text: Regulation 2309/93 created the European Agency for the Evaluation of Medicinal Products, now the European Medicines Agency (EMA), and a single EU-wide authorisation route. Its procedures started on 1 January 1995.

eu-directive-2001-83.title: One EU code for medicines
eu-directive-2001-83.text: Directive 2001/83/EC of 6 November 2001 brought the EU's medicines laws together in one code and repealed Directive 65/65/EEC. Its core rule is unchanged: no medicine on the market without a marketing authorisation.

exenatide-approval.title: Exenatide, a GLP-1 receptor medicine, is approved in the US
exenatide-approval.text: On 28 April 2005 the FDA approved Byetta (exenatide), a synthetic peptide first identified in Gila monster venom.

eu-conditional-authorisation.title: EU conditional marketing authorisation
eu-conditional-authorisation.text: From 2006 the EU could grant a conditional marketing authorisation for medicines that meet an unmet need, on less complete data than normal. It lasts one year at a time and the company must deliver the missing studies.

exenatide-approval-eu.title: Exenatide is authorised in the EU
exenatide-approval-eu.text: On 20 November 2006 the EU authorised Byetta (exenatide). That authorisation was withdrawn at the company's request on 1 January 2026.

nl-geneesmiddelenwet-2007.title: The Dutch Geneesmiddelenwet comes into force
nl-geneesmiddelenwet-2007.text: On 1 July 2007 the Geneesmiddelenwet, the Dutch Medicines Act of 8 February 2007, came into force. It replaced the Wet op de Geneesmiddelenvoorziening of 1958 and sets out the EU rules in Dutch law.

liraglutide-approval.title: Liraglutide is authorised in the EU
liraglutide-approval.text: On 30 June 2009 the EU authorised Victoza (liraglutide). It binds to albumin in the blood and resists breakdown, so one injection a day is enough.

liraglutide-approval-us.title: Liraglutide: a once-daily GLP-1 medicine
liraglutide-approval-us.text: On 25 January 2010 the FDA approved Victoza (liraglutide). It binds to albumin in the blood and resists breakdown, so one injection a day is enough.

tesamorelin-approval.title: Tesamorelin is approved in the US
tesamorelin-approval.text: On 10 November 2010 the FDA approved Egrifta (tesamorelin), an analogue of growth-hormone-releasing factor, to reduce excess belly fat in adults with HIV and lipodystrophy.

afamelanotide-approval.title: Afamelanotide: authorised under exceptional circumstances
afamelanotide-approval.text: On 22 December 2014 the EU authorised Scenesse (afamelanotide), an implant for a rare disease that makes light painful, under 'exceptional circumstances' because full data could not be collected.

ema-prime-launched.title: The EMA starts its PRIME scheme
ema-prime-launched.text: In March 2016 the EMA published the guidance for PRIME, a scheme that gives early advice to developers of medicines for unmet needs to speed up development and review.

semaglutide-approval.title: Semaglutide is approved in the US
semaglutide-approval.text: On 5 December 2017 the FDA approved Ozempic (semaglutide) for type 2 diabetes.

wada-tb500-s2.title: TB-500 named on the doping list
wada-tb500-s2.text: From 1 January 2018 the World Anti-Doping Agency named thymosin beta-4 and its derivatives, such as TB-500, as examples of prohibited growth factors.

semaglutide-approval-eu.title: Semaglutide is authorised in the EU
semaglutide-approval-eu.text: On 8 February 2018 the EU authorised Ozempic (semaglutide) for type 2 diabetes.

bremelanotide-approval.title: Bremelanotide is approved in the US
bremelanotide-approval.text: On 21 June 2019 the FDA approved Vyleesi (bremelanotide), a melanocortin-receptor agonist, for low sexual desire in some premenopausal women.

afamelanotide-approval-us.title: Afamelanotide is approved in the US
afamelanotide-approval-us.text: On 8 October 2019 the FDA approved Scenesse (afamelanotide), an implant for a rare disease that makes light painful.

wegovy-approval.title: Semaglutide for weight management in the US
wegovy-approval.text: On 4 June 2021 the FDA approved Wegovy (semaglutide) for weight management.

wada-bpc157-s0.title: BPC-157 banned in sport
wada-bpc157-s0.text: From 1 January 2022 the World Anti-Doping Agency lists BPC-157 by name under S0, non-approved substances, which are prohibited at all times.

wegovy-approval-eu.title: Semaglutide for weight management in the EU
wegovy-approval-eu.text: On 6 January 2022 the EU authorised Wegovy (semaglutide) for weight management.

glp1-shortages.title: GLP-1 shortages and copies made by US pharmacies
glp1-shortages.text: From 2022 rising demand put semaglutide and tirzepatide injections on the FDA's shortage list. During a shortage, US pharmacies may compound copies, and the FDA later warned of dosing errors with compounded semaglutide.

tirzepatide-approval.title: Tirzepatide is approved in the US
tirzepatide-approval.text: On 13 May 2022 the FDA approved Mounjaro (tirzepatide) for type 2 diabetes. It acts on two hormone receptors, for GLP-1 and GIP.

tirzepatide-approval-eu.title: Tirzepatide is authorised in the EU
tirzepatide-approval-eu.text: On 15 September 2022 the EU authorised Mounjaro (tirzepatide). It acts on two hormone receptors, for GLP-1 and GIP.

fda-category-2-peptides.title: FDA lists peptides as possible safety risks for compounding
fda-category-2-peptides.text: On 29 September 2023 the FDA added peptides such as ipamorelin to 'category 2', bulk substances that may present significant safety risks in compounding. BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV were also in category 2 at some point (the FDA gives no date for them) until their nominations were withdrawn.

falsified-ozempic-alerts.title: Fake Ozempic pens found in Europe
falsified-ozempic-alerts.text: On 18 October 2023 the EMA warned of falsified Ozempic pens, and the Dutch and UK regulators followed within days. In Germany, fake pens were found to contain insulin instead of semaglutide; in the UK, people were taken to hospital with very low blood sugar that pointed to insulin.

falsified-ozempic-uk.title: Fake Ozempic pens in the UK
falsified-ozempic-uk.text: On 26 October 2023 the UK medicines regulator warned of fake Ozempic pens: it had seized 369 potentially fake pens since January 2023. Some people were taken to hospital with very low blood sugar that pointed to insulin in the pens.

zepbound-approval.title: Tirzepatide for weight management in the US
zepbound-approval.text: On 8 November 2023 the FDA approved Zepbound (tirzepatide) for weight management.

who-falsified-alert.title: WHO warns about falsified semaglutide
who-falsified-alert.text: On 20 June 2024 the World Health Organization warned about falsified medicines used for diabetes and weight loss, after falsified Ozempic batches were found in Brazil, the UK and the US.

lasker-glp1.title: Lasker Award for the GLP-1 story
lasker-glp1.text: The 2024 Lasker-DeBakey Clinical Medical Research Award went to Joel Habener and Svetlana Mojsov for the discovery of GLP-1(7-37), and to Lotte Bjerre Knudsen, a Novo Nordisk scientist, for her role in developing long-acting versions to treat obesity.

glp1-shortages-end.title: The US GLP-1 shortages end
glp1-shortages-end.text: The FDA declared the tirzepatide shortage resolved on 2 October 2024 (confirmed on 19 December 2024) and the semaglutide shortage resolved on 21 February 2025. The temporary room for pharmacies to compound copies then ran out in 2025.

unlicensed-supply-seizures.title: Record seizures of unlicensed weight-loss medicines
unlicensed-supply-seizures.text: In January 2026 the UK regulator reported almost 20 million doses of illegal medicines seized in 2025, up from 17 million in 2024, including 5,680 GLP-1 pens. In May 2026 it made its largest seizure of unlicensed weight-loss medicines, including retatrutide and tirzepatide. Vials are also sold online 'for research purposes' without a prescription.

fda-pcac-2026-vote.title: FDA advisers vote on seven peptides
fda-pcac-2026-vote.text: On 23 July 2026 the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted 8–6, with one abstention, to recommend BPC-157 for the 503A list of substances US pharmacies may compound on prescription; of the seven peptides it considered, it recommended six (BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Semax and epitalon, but not emideltide, also called DSIP), as reported from the public meeting. The vote is advisory and non-binding and went against FDA staff's own recommendation, so legal compounding stays prohibited until the FDA formally adopts it and completes rulemaking. None of these peptides is an approved medicine in the US, the UK, Canada or Australia (Semax is registered as a medicine in Russia). A listing would not be a marketing authorisation, would say nothing about whether they work, and would change nothing outside the US.

au-mcbride-letter.title: An Australian doctor links thalidomide to birth defects
au-mcbride-letter.text: In December 1961 William McBride, a doctor in New South Wales, wrote to The Lancet. About 1.5% of babies are born with abnormalities, he reported, but he had seen multiple severe abnormalities in almost 20% of babies born to women given thalidomide in pregnancy.

ca-thalidomide-withdrawn.title: Thalidomide is taken off the market in Canada
ca-thalidomide-withdrawn.text: Thalidomide had been licensed in Canada as a prescription medicine. It was removed from the market in 1962. A 1963 report counted 115 children born in Canada in 1961 and 1962 with malformations linked to thalidomide taken by their mothers in early pregnancy.

uk-committee-on-safety-of-drugs.title: The UK sets up a Committee on Safety of Drugs
uk-committee-on-safety-of-drugs.text: After thalidomide, the UK government accepted an expert report and set up an independent Committee on Safety of Drugs. It was to judge the toxicity tests of a new drug before trials in people, and the trials before general use, and to collect reports of side effects. At first the scheme was voluntary.

au-drug-evaluation-committee.title: Australia appoints a drug evaluation committee
au-drug-evaluation-committee.text: On 3 June 1963 the Australian Drug Evaluation Committee was appointed: a committee of independent experts to advise on the safety of medicines.

uk-yellow-card.title: The UK Yellow Card scheme starts
uk-yellow-card.text: In the wake of thalidomide, the UK began to collect reports of suspected side effects of medicines through the Yellow Card scheme, as an early warning of possible hazards. It was introduced by Sir Derrick Dunlop, chair of the Committee on Safety of Drugs.

au-adverse-reaction-reporting.title: Australia starts collecting side-effect reports
au-adverse-reaction-reporting.text: In August 1964 Australia's scheme for reporting suspected side effects of medicines started. By December 1966 it had received 760 reports.

ca-adverse-reaction-reporting.title: Canada starts collecting side-effect reports
ca-adverse-reaction-reporting.text: From 1965 Canada's national health department collected reports of suspected side effects of medicines. Today this is Health Canada's Canada Vigilance Program.

uk-medicines-act-1968.title: The UK Medicines Act puts licensing into law
uk-medicines-act-1968.text: The Medicines Act 1968 received Royal Assent on 25 October 1968. Its Part II set up licences and certificates for medicinal products in UK law.

au-therapeutic-goods-act.title: Australia's Therapeutic Goods Act takes effect
au-therapeutic-goods-act.text: On 15 February 1991 the Therapeutic Goods Act 1989 took effect. It set up the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG), run by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA). Before a medicine is registered, the TGA must judge whether its quality, safety and efficacy have been satisfactorily established.

uk-mhra-formed.title: The MHRA is formed
uk-mhra-formed.text: On 1 April 2003 the Medicines Control Agency and the Medical Devices Agency merged into today's UK regulator, the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA).

tesamorelin-approval-ca.title: Tesamorelin is approved in Canada
tesamorelin-approval-ca.text: On 29 April 2014 Health Canada approved Egrifta (tesamorelin) for excess belly fat in adults with HIV and lipodystrophy, under restrictions, after an expert panel reconsidered an earlier refusal. It was sold from June 2015.

semaglutide-approval-ca.title: Semaglutide is approved in Canada
semaglutide-approval-ca.text: On 4 January 2018 Health Canada approved Ozempic (semaglutide), the first semaglutide medicine in Canada.

semaglutide-approval-au.title: Semaglutide is approved in Australia
semaglutide-approval-au.text: On 28 August 2019 Ozempic (semaglutide) was registered in Australia for type 2 diabetes.

wegovy-approval-uk.title: Wegovy is licensed in the UK
wegovy-approval-uk.text: On 24 September 2021 the UK medicines regulator licensed Wegovy (semaglutide) pens for Great Britain.

tirzepatide-approval-uk.title: Tirzepatide is licensed in the UK
tirzepatide-approval-uk.text: On 26 September 2022 the UK medicines regulator granted the first Great Britain licences for Mounjaro (tirzepatide) pens.

tesamorelin-ca-no-longer-sold.title: Tesamorelin is no longer sold in Canada
tesamorelin-ca-no-longer-sold.text: On 30 September 2022 Health Canada cancelled the drug identification number of the only Egrifta (tesamorelin) product sold in Canada, after the company told Health Canada it had stopped selling it. Tesamorelin is still approved in the US.

tirzepatide-approval-ca.title: Tirzepatide is approved in Canada
tirzepatide-approval-ca.text: On 24 November 2022 Health Canada approved Mounjaro (tirzepatide). It acts on two hormone receptors, for GLP-1 and GIP.

tirzepatide-approval-au.title: Tirzepatide is approved in Australia
tirzepatide-approval-au.text: On 23 December 2022 Mounjaro (tirzepatide) was registered in Australia for type 2 diabetes.

au-bpc-157-schedule-4.title: BPC-157 becomes a prescription-only medicine in Australia
au-bpc-157-schedule-4.text: From 1 June 2024 BPC-157 is in Schedule 4 of Australia's Poisons Standard, the schedule for prescription-only medicines, with an entry that prohibits possession without authorisation. The TGA had received 48 referrals for imports of BPC-157 since July 2022.

uk-illicit-factory-retatrutide.title: An illegal weight-loss pen factory is shut down in the UK
uk-illicit-factory-retatrutide.text: The UK regulator shut down an illegal factory making weight-loss pens and seized thousands of unlicensed retatrutide and tirzepatide pens. Retatrutide is still being tested and is not approved in the UK.

ca-peptides-advisory-2026.title: Health Canada warns about injecting unauthorised peptides
ca-peptides-advisory-2026.text: Health Canada warned that unauthorised injectable peptides from the internet can seriously harm people. It listed peptides it had seized, such as BPC-157, CJC-1295, ipamorelin, TB-500 and retatrutide. Unauthorised drug products are illegal in Canada and have not been assessed for safety, efficacy and quality, and a 'research use only' label does not make them legal.

au-peptides-compliance-priority.title: Australia makes unapproved peptides a compliance priority
au-peptides-compliance-priority.text: The TGA added unapproved peptide products to its priority areas for enforcement, after detecting more unlawful importation, supply and advertising. Its responses may include infringement notices, seizures, import interventions and civil or criminal penalties.

uk-counterfeit-pens-2026.title: Fake weight-loss pens seized in Birmingham
uk-counterfeit-pens-2026.text: On 14 October 2026 the UK regulator and police seized more than 12,000 fake retatrutide and tirzepatide pens in Birmingham, with packaging for about 30,000 more. Retatrutide has not been authorised for use in the UK.
